g.text: Large language models encode vast amounts of factual knowledge in their
parameters, but this knowledge can become outdated or incorrect over time.
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Large language models encode vast amounts of factual knowledge in their parameters, but this knowledge can become outdated or incorrect over time.

g.text: Model editing has emerged as a promising approach to update specific facts
without expensive full retraining (Zhang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023).
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=2) Model editing has emerged as a promising approach to update specific facts without expensive full retraining (Zhang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023).

g.text: Methods such as ROME (Meng et al., 2022a) and MEMIT (Meng et al.,
2022b) directly modify model weights to insert new knowledge,
while memory-based approaches like MEND (Mitchell et al., 2021)
and SERAC (Mitchell et al., 2022) learn to…
g.title: N3 [Prior_Work] (cites=4) Methods such as ROME (Meng et al., 2022a) and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2022b) directly modify model weights to insert new knowledge, while memory-based approaches like MEND (Mitchell et al., 2021) and SERAC (Mitchell et al., 2022) learn to predict weight updates or store edits externally.

g.text: Fine-tuning-based editing offers a simpler alternative: directly optimizing
a subset of model parameters on the edit examples (Yang et al., 2025b).
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Fine-tuning-based editing offers a simpler alternative: directly optimizing a subset of model parameters on the edit examples (Yang et al., 2025b).

g.text: This approach achieves competitive editing performance while avoiding the
g.title: N5 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) This approach achieves competitive editing performance while avoiding the complexity of specialized editing networks.

g.text: However, a critical design choice remains: which layer should be
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, a critical design choice remains: which layer should be fine-tuned?

g.text: Current practice relies on model-specific heuristics—early-middle
layers for some architectures, late-middle layers for
others—determined through expensive layer sweeps (Yang et al.,
g.title: N7pw [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Current practice relies on model-specific heuristics—early-middle layers for some architectures, late-middle layers for others—determined through expensive layer sweeps (Yang et al., 2025b).

g.text: These heuristics lack principled justification and must be
re-tuned for each new model family.
g.title: N7 [Limitation] (cites=0) These heuristics lack principled justification and must be re-tuned for each new model family.

g.text: In this paper, we investigate whether gradient information can provide a
g.title: N8 [Method] (cites=0) In this paper, we investigate whether gradient information can provide a principled basis for layer selection.

g.text: We propose GradRatio-Select, which computes the ratio of edit-to-retain
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=0) We propose GradRatio-Select, which computes the ratio of edit-to-retain gradient magnitudes across layers: S(ℓ) = ∥gedit (ℓ)∥2 /∥gretain (ℓ)∥2 .

g.text: The intuition is that an ideal editing layer should be responsive to the
edit objective (large edit gradient) while having minimal impact on general
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) The intuition is that an ideal editing layer should be responsive to the edit objective (large edit gradient) while having minimal impact on general capabilities (small retain gradient).

g.text: We further introduce an adaptive threshold to exclude structurally critical
early layers that would cause catastrophic capability loss if modified.
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) We further introduce an adaptive threshold to exclude structurally critical early layers that would cause catastrophic capability loss if modified.

g.text: Our experiments on Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA-3-8B reveal that GradRatio-Select
automatically identifies layers adjacent to manually-tuned heuristics.
g.title: N12 [Result] (cites=0) Our experiments on Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA-3-8B reveal that GradRatio-Select automatically identifies layers adjacent to manually-tuned heuristics.

g.text: On Qwen2.5-7B, the method achieves performance statistically
g.title: N13 [Result] (cites=0) On Qwen2.5-7B, the method achieves performance statistically indistinguishable from the baseline.

g.text: However, on LLaMA-3-8B, it shows a 5.26 percentage point capability
degradation, primarily driven by mathematical reasoning tasks.
g.title: N14 [Result] (cites=0) However, on LLaMA-3-8B, it shows a 5.26 percentage point capability degradation, primarily driven by mathematical reasoning tasks.

g.text: These results suggest that while gradient-based selection can automate layer
identification, it does not improve upon carefully-tuned heuristics.
g.title: N15 [Result] (cites=0) These results suggest that while gradient-based selection can automate layer identification, it does not improve upon carefully-tuned heuristics.

g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We propose GradRatio scoring, a gradient-based metric for evaluating layer editability based on the ratio of edit-to-retain gradient magnitudes.

structurally critical early layers, preventing capability
g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We introduce an adaptive threshold mechanism that excludes structurally critical early layers, preventing capability catastrophe.

LLaMA-3-8B, demonstrating that gradient-based selection provides
g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We provide empirical evaluation showing that GradRatio-Select matches heuristic performance on Qwen2.5-7B but underperforms on LLaMA-3-8B, demonstrating that gradient-based selection provides automation without improvement.
